thread.title: Downtown DASH bus route drawing mixed reviews - NewsBreak
thread.title_full: Downtown DASH bus route drawing mixed reviews - NewsBreak

author: Tessa Kresch
title: Downtown DASH bus route drawing mixed reviews - NewsBreak
text:
By Tessa Kresch ,
6 hours ago
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. (WOOD) — It’s been three months since the Downtown Area Shuttle bus in downtown Grand Rapids shortened its route and the change is getting mixed reviews from riders.
The new route was introduced as part of a one-year pilot program aimed at cutting costs and improving efficiency around downtown event spaces. The shortened route focuses more heavily on downtown destinations, including the Acrisure Amphitheater, Van Andel Arena and the future Amway Stadium.
City officials hoped the change to the free downtown area shuttle would encourage more people to use it to attend major events. However, overall DASH ridership has dropped by around 60% since the change.
For some regular riders, the shortened route means the DASH no longer takes them as close to their destinations as it once did.
Scott Melinn, who has been a regular DASH rider for the several months, said the change has added several blocks to his trip home and has prevented him from supporting the businesses he used to love. Melinn, who uses a wheelchair, said there are places along the old route he can no longer reach.
“I now have to get off on Cherry and I have to roll up like three blocks, three city blocks, and then up the hill just to go home,” Melinn said. “There are so many places we just can’t go to anymore.”
Gregory Haynes has been riding the DASH since it started. He said he has noticed more empty seats since the route changed.
“It ain’t got the people who used to ride it,” Haynes said. “It’s empty. It’s a waste of gas.”
Haynes said the bus still gets much busier on concert nights or if there are any major events in town but is often less crowded outside of major events.
Mobile GR Strategic Initiatives Manager Max Gilles said the drop in overall ridership needs to be considered, alongside the reduction in DASH service.
Service hours and investment in the program were reduced as part of the route change.
“Total ridership is down, but there was a roughly 50% reduction in service hours and investment into the service. So that is expected,” Gilles said.
He also said event-related DASH ridership has increased significantly, which was one of the goals of the shortened route.
“A lot of the intention around this was to encourage event traffic and usage of this service,” Gilles said. “We’ve seen a drastic increase in that.”
The DASH also increased its frequency downtown, going from buses every 15 minutes to every eight minutes.
Gilles said it is still too early to determine the full impact of the new route.
The city plans to look at ridership data quarterly rather than relying solely on month-to-month numbers.
But officials also want to hear directly from riders.
“We can look at data all we want but ultimately, we want to hear from the community and see how they feel it’s going,” Gilles said.
Dozens of people have already reached out to Mobile GR with concerns about the route change. The city plans to begin sending out surveys to those who have reached out and also using QR codes this month to collect additional feedback from DASH riders.
Gilles said the goal is to understand whether the increased frequency downtown is helping residents and commuters while still supporting people traveling to events.
